chain.g: a happening, accident, symptom of disease

ety.text: From Middle English sinthoma, from Medieval Latin sinthoma, altered by Late Latin symptoma, from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma, “a happening, accident, symptom of disease”), from stem of συμπίπτω (sumpíptō, “Ι befall”), from συν- (sun-, “together”) + πίπτω (píptō, “to fall”). See also syn-, -oma, -ome.

senses.d: A perceived change in some function, sensation or appearance of a person that indicates a disease or disorder, such as fever, headache or rash; strictly, a symptom is felt or experienced by the patient, while a sign can be detected by an observer.
ex: The doctor told that his coughing and sneezing was the symptom of standing for too long in the rain.
Swollen breasts, morning sickness, and a missed period are classic symptoms of pregnancy.

senses.d: A signal; anything that indicates, or is characteristic of, the presence of something else, especially of something undesirable.
ex: Lying, hiding one's true feelings, and having affairs are typical symptoms of a doomed marriage.
Some people see birth outside of marriage as a social problem—a sign of a breakdown in the traditional family and a symptom of moral decay.

grp.label: something that indicates a disease or disorder

ety.text: From Middle French (sinthome, Bernard de Gordon). Borrowed from Latin symptōma, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma).

es:síntoma.gl: symptom (indicators and characteristics of the presence of something else)

ety.text: From Latin symptōma, from Ancient Greek σύμπτωμα (súmptōma).

Borrowed from Latin indicium, from indicō (“point out, indicate, show”).

ant: Treatment of symptoms versus treatment of cause

senses.d: A character or glyph representing an idea, concept or object.
ex: "$" is the symbol for dollars in the US and some other countries.
Chinese people use word symbols for writing.

senses.d: A thing considered the embodiment or cardinal exemplar of a concept, theme, or other thing.
ex: The lion is the symbol of courage; the lamb is the symbol of meekness or patience.

senses.d: A type of noun whereby the form refers to the same entity independently of the context; a symbol arbitrarily denotes a referent. See also icon and index.
A summary of a dogmatic statement of faith.
ex: The Apostles, Nicene Creed and the confessional books of Protestantism, such as the Augsburg Confession of Lutheranism are considered symbols.

senses.d: The numerical expression which defines a plane's position relative to the assumed axes.
That which is thrown into a common fund; hence, an appointed or accustomed duty.
ex: They do their work in the days of peace […] and come to pay their symbol in a war or in a plague.

senses.d: Share; allotment.
ex: The persons who are to be judged […] shall all appear to receive their symbol.

senses.d: An internal identifier used by a debugger to relate parts of the compiled program to the corresponding names in the source code.
A signalling event on a communications channel; a signal that cannot be further divided into meaningful information.
To symbolize.

Borrowed from Middle French sympathie, from Late Latin sympathīa (“feeling in common”), from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă, “fellow feeling”), from σῠμπᾰθής (sŭmpăthḗs, “affected by like feelings; exerting mutual influence, interacting”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, “-y”, nominal suffix). Equivalent to sym- (“acting or considered together”) + -pathy (“feeling”).

senses.d: A feeling of pity or sorrow for the suffering or distress of another.
The formal expression of pity or sorrow for someone else's misfortune.
The ability to share the feelings of another.
Inclination to think or feel alike; emotional or intellectual accord; common feeling.
ex: Oh vvhat a ſimpathie of vvoe is this, / As farre from helpe, as Lymbo is from bliſſe.

senses.d: Support in the form of shared feelings or opinions.
Feeling of loyalty; tendency towards, agreement with or approval of an opinion or aim; a favorable attitude.
ex: Many people in Hollywood were blacklisted merely because they were suspected of Communist sympathies.

senses.d: An affinity, association or mutual relationship between people or things such that they are correspondingly affected by any condition.
ex: A peculiarity of were-animals is the sympathy that exists between their animal form and that of the human with whom it is connected.
Sympathy likened anything to anything else in universal attraction, e.g. the fate of men to the course of the planets.

senses.d: Mutual or parallel susceptibility or a condition brought about by it.
Artistic harmony, as of shape or colour in a painting.
